idiom_name: impl Iterator<Item = T> with next() -> Option<T>; std::iter::from_fn/successors
implementation_notes: Rust models sequences with the Iterator trait: implementing next() -> Option<T> makes a type a lazy producer that for loops and the whole adapter library (map/take/zip/scan) drive, and the loop's break simply drops the iterator, running its destructors. Closure-based producers avoid a hand-written type: std::iter::from_fn(|| ... Option<T>) turns a stateful closure into one, successors(state, f) carries the state explicitly, and repeat_with covers stateless generation; gen blocks (the keyword is reserved in edition 2024) remain a nightly feature, so they are not a stable realization yet.
pitfalls: next takes &mut self, so an iterator is mutable state: moving it into a helper while also reading it elsewhere does not compile, and cloning an iterator whose Clone shares state (Rc, file handles) can duplicate or invalidate elements - borrow with by_ref() instead.
Adapters are lazy and inert until consumed: a chain with no for/collect/sum silently does nothing, and a consumed iterator is gone; re-create the source or collect when a second pass is needed.

size_hint is a hint, not a contract: adapters such as filter and scan report bounds that can be wrong, and code that assumes ExactSizeIterator (for example slice indexing) panics rather than degrading.

variants.name: Async stream (futures::Stream)
variants.implementation_notes: Asynchronous production is modelled by the futures-core Stream trait: next() is an async method resolving to Option<T>, consumed with while let Some(x) = stream.next().await or the StreamExt adapters, and implemented by the async-stream crate's stream! macro, a hand-written state machine, or combinators such as stream::unfold. Use it when each element depends on awaited I/O or a timer, and let cancellation be drop-based: dropping the stream drops the in-flight future at its next await point.
pitfalls: A stream is driven by an executor: dropping it cancels at the next await point, but a resource held across an await is only released by the future's Drop, so leaking the future (std::mem::forget, reference cycles) hangs the producer.
Hand-written Stream impls must store and wake the Waker; forgetting to return Poll::Pending with a registered waker produces a task that never wakes - a silent stall with no error.
